paraphrase: Calm abiding is achieved by abandoning the five faults — laziness, forgetting the instruction, laxity and excitement, non-application (of the antidote), and over-application — through the eight antidotes: faith, aspiration, effort and pliancy (against laziness), mindfulness, introspective alertness, application, and equanimity.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Calm abiding is achieved only when, after the ninth state, mental and then physical pliancy arise with their joy and, that joy settling, the mind rests stably on its object at will; before that one has only a likeness of calm abiding.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Both calm abiding and insight are needed: calm abiding is a mind stably placed on its object without distraction, insight is the wisdom analysing the object; like a lamp that is both bright and unflickering, the view of reality needs both.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The nine mental states are achieved in order: placing the mind, continuous placement, repeated placement, close placement, taming, pacifying, thorough pacifying, one-pointedness and equipoise; by six powers (hearing, reflection, mindfulness, alertness, effort and complete familiarity) and four attentions (tight focus, interrupted, uninterrupted and spontaneous).
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The prerequisites of calm abiding are living in a suitable place, having few desires, contentment, not having many activities, pure ethics, and completely abandoning conceptual thoughts such as desire.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Subtle laxity — where the mind stays on its object with some clarity but its intensity of clarity has slackened — is hard to recognise and is often mistaken for flawless meditation; meditating in it long makes the mind dull and forgetful, and it must be recognised and removed by alertness.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: After training in the paths common to sūtra and tantra, one should certainly enter the Vajrayāna, which is far superior to the other vehicles; one then receives empowerment from a qualified master, guards the vows and commitments as one's life, and trains in the two stages.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Having generated bodhicitta, take the bodhisattva vow and train in the deeds: the six perfections to ripen one's own continuum and the four ways of gathering to ripen others.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The only door to the Mahāyāna is the mind of awakening: when it arises one becomes a bodhisattva even without other qualities, and when it is lost one falls from the Mahāyāna even with them; so its benefits must be contemplated.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The training in equalizing and exchanging self and other, taught by Śāntideva: considering the faults of self-cherishing and the benefits of cherishing others, one exchanges the objects of cherishing — cherishing others as one used to cherish oneself.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Having trained the mind, adopt the aspiring mind of awakening by ritual, and guard it by the precepts (remembering its benefits, generating it six times a day, not abandoning beings, gathering the accumulations, and abandoning the four black and adopting the four white dharmas).
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The sevenfold instruction of cause and effect, from Atiśa's lineage: on the basis of equanimity, (1) recognising all beings as one's mothers, (2) remembering their kindness, (3) wishing to repay it, (4) love, (5) compassion, (6) the extraordinary resolve to take responsibility oneself, and (7) the mind of awakening — the first six being causes and the seventh the effect.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Things lack inherent existence yet exist conventionally as mere designations; because they are dependently arisen they are empty, and because they are empty they can function — the emptiness of inherent existence and the working of cause and effect are one meaning.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Calm abiding alone does not cut the root of saṃsāra — even non-Buddhist sages attain it and still are reborn; the root, grasping at self, is cut only by the wisdom that realizes selflessness.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Just as, to know that a person is absent, one must know the person who is absent, so to realise selflessness one must first correctly identify the self that is to be negated; the object of negation is inherent existence — existence by way of the object's own nature, not posited by the force of conceptual designation. If this is not identified, one's negation will either go too far or not far enough.
notes: Tsongkhapa cites Bodhicaryāvatāra 9.140 ('without contacting the imagined thing, its non-existence is not apprehended'); that verse is not yet a teaching entry in U40. Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The Svātantrikas accept that things have an own-character (inherent nature) conventionally and therefore use autonomous inferences whose subject appears alike to both parties; the Prāsaṅgikas accept no inherent nature even conventionally, so no subject is established in that way and they lead the opponent to the view by consequences and inferences 'renowned to the other'.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: To find the view one must rely on the definitive scriptures and on Nāgārjuna's treatises as explained by Buddhapālita and Candrakīrti, whose Prāsaṅgika reading is the final intent.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The selflessness of persons is established by the sevenfold reasoning of the chariot: the self is neither one with nor different from the aggregates, neither their possessor, support nor supported, neither their collection nor their shape — yet it exists as merely designated in dependence on them.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Those who negate too much — holding that Madhyamaka reasoning refutes all existence, cause and effect and valid cognition, so that nothing at all can be asserted — fall into nihilism and cannot establish the path; reasoning analysing the ultimate does not find things, but not being found by such reasoning is not the same as being refuted by it.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Those who negate too little — refuting only a self or entity imagined by philosophical systems while leaving the innate apprehension of inherent existence untouched — cannot cut the root of saṃsāra.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Insight proper is achieved when analytical meditation on selflessness itself induces pliancy, just as placement induced it in calm abiding; when analysis and stabilization are balanced so that analysis enhances stability, calm abiding and insight are united.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Some claim that all conceptual analysis obstructs meditation and that one should only rest the mind without thought; this is mistaken. Topics such as faith, the value of the human life, impermanence and bodhicitta must be cultivated by analytical meditation that repeatedly examines with discernment, while calm abiding is cultivated by placement meditation; both are meditation.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The teaching of the stages of the path has four greatnesses: through it one understands all the teachings as free of contradiction; all the scriptures dawn as personal instructions; one easily finds the Conqueror's intent; and one is saved from the great wrong of abandoning the dharma.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Contemplate the human life of leisure and endowment — free of the eight unfree states and possessing the ten endowments — its great value (for temporary and final aims), and how difficult it is to find (by its causes, by example and by number); then resolve to take its essence.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: How to conduct a meditation session: the six preparatory practices (cleaning the place and setting up images, arranging offerings, sitting in the proper posture with refuge and bodhicitta, visualizing the field of merit, offering the seven limbs and the maṇḍala, and making requests); then the main topic of meditation; then dedication; between sessions, guarding the senses, eating moderately and so on.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The root of the path is proper reliance on the spiritual teacher in thought and deed. The qualified teacher of the Mahāyāna has ten qualities (after the Mahāyānasūtrālaṅkāra): disciplined, serene, thoroughly pacified, having more good qualities than the student, energetic, rich in scripture, realized in reality, skilled in speech, loving, and free of weariness in teaching.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The origin of suffering: the afflictions — six root afflictions (attachment, anger, pride, ignorance, doubt, afflicted view) — how they arise from the innate grasping at a self, and how through them karma is accumulated; then how one dies and is reborn through the twelve links.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: When, having contemplated the faults of saṃsāra, one wishes for liberation day and night as a prisoner wishes to escape prison, the mind of renunciation (definite emergence) has arisen.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The person of middling scope contemplates the sufferings of saṃsāra in general — the eight sufferings (birth, ageing, sickness, death, meeting the unpleasant, separation from the pleasant, not getting what one wants, the appropriated aggregates), the six sufferings (uncertainty, insatiability, repeatedly discarding bodies, repeatedly taking rebirth, repeated high and low, loneliness) and the three sufferings (of pain, of change, and pervasive conditioning) — and the particular sufferings of each realm.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The path that leads to liberation is the three trainings — ethics, concentration and wisdom — of which ethics is the foundation; one guards it by relying on knowledge of the precepts, a pure mind, shame and conscience, and respect.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Mindfulness of death: death is certain (nothing can stop the Lord of Death, life cannot be extended and continuously runs out, and even while alive there is little time for dharma); the time of death is uncertain (lifespan in this world is not fixed, the causes of death are many and of life few, the body is fragile); at death nothing but dharma helps (not wealth, friends or body). Hence resolve to practise, to practise now, and to practise purely.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Karma has four general characteristics: it is certain (virtue brings happiness, non-virtue suffering), it grows greatly, one does not meet the result of what one has not done, and what is done is not lost. The ten non-virtuous paths and their fully-ripened, cause-similar and environmental results are to be understood, and wrongdoing purified by the four powers (repudiation/regret, reliance, the remedy, and restraint from repeating).
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Reflect on the sufferings of the hells, the hungry ghosts and animals as where one will go after death if one does not practise.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Going for refuge arises from two causes — fear of the lower realms and faith that the Three Jewels can protect; one knows the qualities of Buddha, Dharma and Saṅgha, goes for refuge by knowing their differences, by commitment, and without speaking of other refuges, and keeps the precepts of refuge.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.
